title: A Small Park Has a Large Boundary
source_title: Xinhua Headlines: Pocket parks drive urban renewal, eco-improvement efforts in China
source_verification: 页面可访问；核验了口袋公园盘活闲置地、遮阴通风与微气候调节，公私协作运营且部分收入用于维护，以及入户访谈和社区协商参与规划等事实。
adaptation_note: 题材参考所列新华社英文网公开事实；本站原创改写，非媒体原文，非历年真题。
content:
Pocket parks are praised for achieving much with little land. A vacant lot can become shade during a heat wave, a place for exercise and a setting where neighbors meet. Because the projects are small, they can be inserted into old districts that lack space for a conventional park. Their apparent simplicity, however, can obscure how far their effects extend beyond the fence.

Cooling is one example. Trees and planned airflow may reduce heat inside the site, but the benefit depends on surrounding pavement, building shadows and whether residents can walk there safely during the hottest hours. Social use has similar spillovers. Evening activity can support nearby shops and improve passive observation of the street, while noise or tourist traffic may burden adjacent homes. A park is therefore better understood as an intervention in a local system than as a decorated parcel.

This perspective changes participation. Asking residents to choose equipment from a catalog is too late and too narrow. Consultation should identify who currently uses the vacant land, which routes cross it, when shade is needed and what memories attach to the place. Children, older residents, cleaners, nearby tenants and street businesses may value different outcomes. Their claims cannot all be maximized, so planners should publish trade-offs rather than presenting the final design as unanimous community preference.

Operations create another boundary. Commercial kiosks can finance maintenance and bring activity, but they may gradually occupy public seating or shift the park toward visitors with greater spending power. A contract should specify protected free space, maintenance duties, revenue use and ways to revise an arrangement that changes the public character of the site.

Even environmental success requires patient evidence. Comparing temperature, biodiversity and use before and after construction is more informative than photographing opening day. Evaluation should include nearby streets, not only sensors placed under new trees.

The value of a pocket park lies precisely in its ability to influence a larger neighborhood. Responsible design follows those influences outward—to heat, movement, commerce, memory and access—and remains accountable for both benefits and costs.

title: A Mailbox Is Not Yet a Conversation
source_title: ChineseToday | Minzhu Village's path to grassroots democracy
source_verification: 页面可访问；核验了城市更新中的院坝会、由1953年工厂意见箱演变的“一号邮箱”线上线下渠道，人大代表实地调研，以及社区服务费率协商等事实。
adaptation_note: 题材参考所列新华社英文网公开事实；本站原创改写，非媒体原文，非历年真题。
content:
A suggestion box makes participation visible. Its presence tells residents that officials expect to hear from them, and a digital version can lower the cost of submitting an idea. Yet the democratic value of such a channel is not contained in the box. It emerges from the chain of attention, deliberation, decision and explanation that follows a message.

The first challenge is representation. People confident with writing or mobile tools are more likely to submit detailed proposals. Renters, shift workers, people with disabilities or residents who distrust formal channels may remain quiet. Courtyard meetings and field visits can broaden the evidence, but their timing, accessibility and facilitation still shape who speaks. Officials should treat silence as missing information rather than consent.

The second challenge is selection. Thousands of suggestions cannot all receive the same response. Some concern urgent safety repairs; others involve fees, shared spaces or conflicting preferences. A fair system needs published categories, response deadlines and reasons for closing or combining proposals. Otherwise, quick solutions to simple issues can produce an impressive completion rate while difficult structural complaints disappear from view.

Deliberation adds more than volume. When residents discuss a service fee with property managers, they hear constraints and alternatives rather than only sending separate demands. This can reveal whether a disagreement concerns facts, distribution or trust. But meetings should not be used to wear down opposition until apparent agreement appears. Records need to show whose interests remain affected.

Feedback completes the loop. A resident whose proposal is rejected may still regard the process as legitimate if the evidence and rule are clear, whereas an accepted idea followed by unexplained delay can deepen distrust. Publishing outcomes also lets the wider community examine whether certain streets or groups receive faster attention.

A mailbox is thus infrastructure for democracy in the same way that a station is infrastructure for transport: it creates an entry point, not a completed journey. The quality of governance depends on whether different people can enter, trace where their concern goes and challenge the route when it repeatedly leads nowhere.

title: A Target Needs a Path Between Services
source_title: China unveils five-year plan to improve services, quality of life for people with disabilities
source_verification: 页面可访问；核验了残疾人就业、康复服务和医疗参保目标，公共场馆与自助终端无障碍改造，全国残疾人抽样调查数据更新，以及人工智能与辅助技术应用等事实。
adaptation_note: 题材参考所列新华社英文网公开事实；本站原创改写，非媒体原文，非历年真题。
content:
A five-year disability plan can specify jobs created, rehabilitation coverage, insurance participation and accessible facilities. Each target directs attention and funding, but people experience the system across categories. A student needs accessible transport to reach an inclusive school. A trained graduate needs recruitment, workplace adjustment and a complaint channel. A rehabilitation device may be clinically suitable yet unusable if repair, payment or digital instructions are missing.

This interdependence makes handoffs a critical measure of quality. Agencies often report the service they deliver, while the gap between two services belongs to nobody. A person may complete skills training but receive no introduction to employers prepared to make adjustments. A hospital may prescribe an assistive device without confirming that the home or school can accommodate it. Plans should assign responsibility for such transitions and record whether the next step actually occurred.

Data can reveal where pathways break, provided that categories are designed carefully. National surveys help update population needs, while service records show participation. Yet a high enrollment rate does not indicate whether education is accessible, and an employment count does not reveal pay, stability or career progression. Measures should be disaggregated by location, gender, age and disability type without publishing information that identifies individuals. People with disabilities should help decide which outcomes matter and how burdensome data collection feels.

Technology introduces another handoff—from prototype to daily use. Artificial intelligence or robotics may expand independence, but public trials should test safety, repairability and compatibility with ordinary services. Innovation funding should not draw resources away from reliable low-tech supports such as sign-language access, readable forms or human assistance at self-service terminals.

Ambitious targets are valuable when they organize action rather than decorate a report. Their real achievement lies in the routes connecting education, care, work, culture and legal protection. A plan succeeds not when every office completes its own column, but when a person can move through the columns without repeatedly starting again.

title: Rights Become Real at the Service Counter
source_title: China Focus: China targets stronger livelihood, employment support for people with disabilities
source_verification: 页面可访问；核验了残疾人保障法修订和无障碍环境建设法地方落实，司法保护、法律援助与无障碍公共法律服务，以及全生命周期教育就业和康复支持等事实。
adaptation_note: 题材参考所列新华社英文网公开事实；本站原创改写，非媒体原文，非历年真题。
content:
A legal right to accessible services is essential, but its practical meaning appears in ordinary encounters. Can a blind applicant read the employment form? Will a court provide sign-language interpretation without treating it as a personal favor? Can a person with an intellectual disability understand a guardianship decision and challenge abuse? The distance between written protection and these moments is the work of implementation.

Implementation begins with duties that can be identified. A public agency should know which accessibility standard applies, who funds an adjustment and how quickly a barrier must be removed. Frontline employees need training, but responsibility cannot be transferred entirely to their goodwill. Accessible formats, interpretation budgets and escalation procedures must be built into normal operations. Otherwise, courteous staff may improvise inconsistent solutions, while an unfriendly employee can make a formal right disappear.

Remedies matter because prevention will sometimes fail. Legal aid needs accessible intake, confidentiality and professionals familiar with disability-related discrimination. Complaint systems should allow assistance without taking control away from the complainant. Deadlines must account for continuing harm: a student excluded for a semester or an applicant who loses a job opportunity cannot be fully repaired by a favorable answer years later.

Monitoring also presents a tension. Authorities need evidence about recurring barriers and case outcomes, but public reporting can expose sensitive health or family information in a small community. Anonymous statistics should be paired with audits and consultation rather than detailed stories published without meaningful consent. Independent review helps distinguish a rare error from a repeated institutional pattern.

Law reform and local rules can clarify standards, yet enforcement should remain open to learning. Technologies, workplaces and family arrangements change, creating barriers that earlier texts did not name. Courts, service agencies and organizations of people with disabilities need channels for feeding those experiences back into guidance.

Rights are not weakened by attention to procedure; they are made usable through it. A strong legal framework reaches the ramp, classroom, workplace and service counter, gives officials a defined obligation, and gives the affected person a timely way to demand correction.

title: Accessibility Fails at the Handoff
source_title: China rolls out new measures to improve air travel for passengers with disabilities
source_verification: 页面可访问；核验了民航无障碍服务覆盖下车点、值机、安检、候机、登机、机上服务、离机、行李提取和接机点的全链条一致支持要求。
adaptation_note: 题材参考所列新华社英文网公开事实；本站原创改写，非媒体原文，非历年真题。
content:
Air travel is a chain of services that passengers usually experience as one journey. For a traveler who needs wheelchair assistance, sign-language communication or extra time, the chain becomes visible whenever responsibility changes hands. A smooth check-in cannot compensate for an inaccessible shuttle to the aircraft. Careful boarding loses its value if mobility equipment is damaged or no assistant appears at baggage claim.

A full-service standard tries to prevent these breaks by covering the route from terminal drop-off to final pickup. The difficult part is not listing the stages but allocating accountability across airports, airlines, security contractors and ground handlers. Each organization may meet its internal target while the passenger waits between them. Shared case identifiers, confirmed handoffs and a single contact for disruption can make responsibility traceable without forcing the traveler to repeat medical details at every desk.

Standardization also creates tension. A common minimum reduces arbitrary treatment, yet assistance must remain responsive to individual preference. Some wheelchair users can walk a short distance; others cannot transfer safely. A blind traveler may want navigation guidance without being physically led. Staff should ask rather than infer, and the answer should travel with the service request under clear privacy limits. Consistency means a reliable process for honoring choices, not identical handling of different people.

Disruption is the real test. Weather, gate changes and tight connections compress time, encouraging staff to treat accessibility as optional. Contingency plans should state who rebooks an accessible route, where a person can wait safely and how essential equipment will be located. Performance data must include missed assistance, damaged devices and connection failures, not only passengers successfully boarded. Complaints should trigger reconstruction of the whole journey so recurrent failures at one interface are visible.

Training cannot be a one-time script. Employees need practice with equipment, communication and respectful offers of help, while managers need authority to slow a process that has become unsafe. Travelers and disability organizations should participate in simulations and audits because they recognize risks that departmental checklists normalize.

Seamless service is therefore an institutional property rather than an act of kindness by one employee. Accessibility succeeds when the passenger does not have to manage the organizations that are supposed to manage the journey.

title: The Last Centimeter of a Legal Ramp
source_title: China Focus: Ramp by ramp, China goes barrier-free
source_verification: 页面可访问；核验了入口台阶改坡道的独立出行案例、2023年无障碍环境建设法的普遍受益理念，行人过街延时、低地板公交，以及公益诉讼与残疾人组织参与评估等事实。
adaptation_note: 题材参考所列新华社英文网公开事实；本站原创改写，非媒体原文，非历年真题。
content:
Accessibility law changes the status of a ramp. It is no longer a charitable addition that an owner may provide when convenient, but part of the conditions under which people can participate equally. Yet legal recognition does not settle whether a particular ramp works. A slope may be too steep, a landing blocked, or the accessible entrance locked while the main door remains open. The last centimeter between formal compliance and independent use is where enforcement matters.

Traditional inspection often concentrates on construction documents and measurements at completion. Those checks are indispensable, but real use introduces sequences: reaching the curb cut, crossing before the signal changes, entering a low-floor bus, finding a functioning lift and arriving at a service counter. Failure at one point can cancel success elsewhere. Route-based audits conducted at different times reveal obstacles that isolated facility counts miss.

Enforcement also needs multiple pathways. Regulators can refuse approval for noncompliant projects. Public-interest litigation can address barriers affecting many people, while individual complaints identify daily failures. Disability organizations contribute technical experience and help evaluate whether corrections remain usable after publicity fades. These roles should reinforce rather than replace routine maintenance by the responsible operator. A court order that produces a repaired lift but no inspection schedule may solve the visible case only temporarily.

Universal benefit adds a further policy question. Older people, pregnant women, children and temporarily injured travelers may all use accessible design. This wider value can build political support, but it should not erase the specific rights and expertise of people with disabilities. If officials frame access only as something “everyone may someday need,” current exclusion can become abstract. Direct participation by those facing barriers keeps urgency and accountability visible.

Technology can extend crossing time or announce an accessible bus in real time. It can also introduce opaque failure: a sensor may misread a slow walker, or an app may be inaccessible to the blind passenger it is meant to assist. Digital systems require fallback procedures, bias testing and public reporting just as physical ramps require slope checks.

The purpose of enforcement is not to maximize violations recorded. It is to create dependable routes through ordinary life. Law acquires practical force when standards, user evidence, remedies and maintenance repeatedly converge on that outcome.

questions.explanation: 后文举传感器误判和应用自身不可访问，说明失败机制对用户不透明、难理解。
questions.evidence_text: It can also introduce opaque failure: a sensor may misread a slow walker, or an app may be inaccessible to the blind passenger it is meant to assist.

questions.question: Why does the author prefer route-based audits to facility counts alone?
options: Facility measurements are never legally relevant
One broken link can make several compliant facilities useless together
Routes should be inspected only after complaints
A route contains fewer technical details than a building
questions.explanation: 作者强调出行是连续序列，任一点失败会抵消其他环节成功，故需端到端审计。
questions.evidence_text: Failure at one point can cancel success elsewhere.

questions.question: What risk arises from presenting accessibility only as a universal future need?
options: Older people may stop using accessible design
Public support for maintenance will necessarily disappear
Present exclusion and disabled people's expertise may lose urgency
Legal standards will apply only to temporary injuries
questions.explanation: 第四段警告普遍价值叙事可能抽象化当前排斥，并抹去残疾人的具体权利和经验。
questions.evidence_text: If officials frame access only as something “everyone may someday need,” current exclusion can become abstract.

title: Early Support Without a Narrow Future
source_title: China to expand autism support with early screening, special education programs
source_verification: 页面可访问；核验了0至6岁标准化孤独症筛查和干预、地市级康复救助能力、专门特殊教育学校和贫困家庭子女学前至高中免费教育，以及全生命周期支持等事实。
adaptation_note: 题材参考所列新华社英文网公开事实；本站原创改写，非媒体原文，非历年真题。
content:
Early autism screening can shorten the period in which families know that development differs but cannot obtain an explanation or support. Standardized services for children aged six and under may connect observations in clinics or kindergartens with assessment and intervention. Because younger brains are highly adaptable, timely help can develop communication, daily-living and learning strategies. The ethical value of early action, however, depends on what follows the screen.

Screening is not diagnosis, and diagnosis is not destiny. A brief tool may flag language delay, sensory difference or social behavior that requires fuller evaluation. False reassurance can postpone help, while careless labeling can narrow adults' expectations before they understand the child. Families need clear information about uncertainty, an appeal or second assessment, and services that begin from functional needs rather than a demand to appear typical.

Capacity must also be distributed. Declaring that every city-level region can offer rehabilitation assistance says little about travel time, waiting lists, professional supervision or affordability. Specialist schools may provide expertise for some children, while inclusive classrooms can support participation for others if teachers receive resources and class environments adapt. The policy question is not which setting is universally superior, but whether placement follows an individual assessment and remains reviewable as the child changes.

Life-cycle language is important because childhood intervention cannot be the endpoint. Adolescents need social, academic and mental-health support; adults may need vocational preparation, supported employment, housing choices or assistance with decision-making. A system that invests heavily before age six and then withdraws at graduation transfers risk back to families. Transitions between health, education and employment agencies should have named coordinators and measurable continuity.

Autistic people and family organizations should participate in program design, but representation requires care. The most confident speaker cannot stand for every communication style or support level. Consultation may need alternative formats, supported communication and separate routes for children, adults and caregivers to express different interests. Outcome measures should include well-being, autonomy and participation rather than only reduction of visible behaviors.

Early support is most defensible when it expands possible futures. It should give a child and family more tools, timely services and better choices without pretending that one screening result has already written the life ahead.

questions.question: What ethical condition does the passage attach to early autism screening?
options: It should determine a child's permanent educational placement
It should focus mainly on eliminating visible behaviors
It can replace comprehensive assessment when used before age six
It must lead to uncertain-aware, individualized and continuing support
questions.explanation: 文章强调筛查非诊断、安置需个别评估、支持需贯穿生命周期且衡量自主与福祉。
questions.evidence_text: The ethical value of early action, however, depends on what follows the screen.

questions.question: What should families receive when an assessment remains uncertain?
options: Clear information, a route to another assessment and needs-based support
A permanent special-school placement
A guarantee that no future support will be needed
Only a score showing visible behaviors
questions.explanation: 第二段明确要求告知不确定性、申诉或二次评估，并从功能需要出发提供服务。
questions.evidence_text: Families need clear information about uncertainty, an appeal or second assessment, and services that begin from functional needs rather than a demand to appear typical.

questions.question: What does “reviewable” mean when discussing school placement?
options: Published as a public ranking
Able to be reconsidered as needs change
Decided by one screening result
Limited to children in specialist schools
questions.explanation: 语境说儿童会变化，安置应随个别评估重新审视，故指可复核调整。
questions.evidence_text: placement follows an individual assessment and remains reviewable as the child changes.

questions.question: Why does the author question city-level service capacity figures?
options: Every city should use the same intervention method
Travel time is unrelated to real access
Nominal availability may conceal distance, queues, cost or weak supervision
Specialist schools provide rehabilitation in every region
questions.explanation: 第三段列出时间、等待、督导和费用，说明宣布具备能力不等于家庭可获得高质量服务。
questions.evidence_text: Declaring that every city-level region can offer rehabilitation assistance says little about travel time, waiting lists, professional supervision or affordability.

questions.question: What is the danger of ending intensive support after childhood?
options: Early intervention becomes scientifically invalid
Adults no longer require any communication support
Schools must take responsibility for employment indefinitely
Unmanaged transition risks are shifted back to individuals and families
questions.explanation: 作者指出毕业后撤回支持会把风险重新转给家庭，并主张跨部门连续衔接。
questions.evidence_text: A system that invests heavily before age six and then withdraws at graduation transfers risk back to families.

title: A Standard Is a Compressed Public Argument
source_title: New batch of national standards takes effect in China
source_verification: 页面可访问；核验了光伏电站保护与远程监测、多式联运服务保障和评价指标、旅游船服务质量要求、茶供应链全环节管理，以及2025年国家标准发布数量等事实。
adaptation_note: 题材参考所列新华社英文网公开事实；本站原创改写，非媒体原文，非历年真题。
content:
A technical standard can look like neutral detail: a formula for evaluating multimodal transport, a requirement for photovoltaic protection equipment, or a list of service conditions on a tour boat. In fact, each document compresses choices about acceptable risk, measurable quality and who bears the cost of failure. The apparent precision of a number should not conceal the public argument embedded within it.

Measurement boundaries are one source of judgment. A transport standard may calculate punctuality at transfer points, yet exclude the time a passenger spends finding an inaccessible connection. A tourism rule may count trained staff without asking whether interpretation reaches visitors with hearing loss. What is omitted can guide investment just as strongly as what is included, because organizations optimize the indicators against which they are audited.

Standards must also balance compatibility and innovation. Common terminology and interfaces allow suppliers, inspectors and users to communicate. If requirements freeze one existing technology, however, a safer method may face unnecessary barriers. Performance-based language can leave room for alternatives, but it demands competent testing and may create uncertainty for smaller firms. A revision process should therefore publish evidence, transition periods and reasons for changing thresholds.

Implementation produces distributional effects. Compliance costs may improve safety while raising prices or pushing small operators from a market. That does not prove a requirement is mistaken; it means policymakers should examine assistance, phased deadlines and whether the same public outcome can be achieved less burdensomely. Exemptions need care because the people served by low-cost operators should not receive systematically weaker protection.

Participation is difficult but necessary. Technical committees need engineers and industry experience, while consumers, workers and affected communities identify consequences that laboratory tests miss. Drafts should be available in understandable summaries, not only specialist language. Complaints and accident data after implementation should feed revision rather than being treated as evidence that users failed to follow instructions.

A standard succeeds when it creates dependable coordination and learning, not merely uniform paperwork. Its authority comes from technical rigor, transparent judgment and willingness to correct the boundary between what society currently accepts and what better evidence shows it should demand.

questions.question: Why does the author call a standard a “compressed public argument”?
options: It contains contestable choices about risk, quality, cost and measurement
It should be written only by elected officials
It summarizes every consumer complaint in one formula
It removes judgment by using precise numbers
questions.explanation: 全文说明指标边界、技术路径、成本分配和参与均包含价值选择，标准并非纯中性细节。
questions.evidence_text: In fact, each document compresses choices about acceptable risk, measurable quality and who bears the cost of failure.

questions.question: What should a revision process disclose?
options: Only the identities of technical committee members
Evidence, transition periods and reasons for threshold changes
A permanent exemption for small operators
Instructions blaming users for every accident
questions.explanation: 第三段明确列出修订过程应公开证据、过渡期与阈值变化理由。
questions.evidence_text: A revision process should therefore publish evidence, transition periods and reasons for changing thresholds.

questions.question: What does “distributional” refer to in paragraph four?
options: How documents are sent to inspectors
How products move through a supply chain
How costs and benefits fall differently across groups
How formulas are divided into smaller steps
questions.explanation: 后文讨论价格、小经营者和低成本服务用户承受不同影响，故指成本收益在人群间的分布。
questions.evidence_text: Implementation produces distributional effects.

questions.question: Why can omitted indicators influence investment?
options: Unmeasured outcomes are always impossible to improve
Technical committees prohibit inaccessible connections
Every organization chooses its own standard
Organizations may neglect outcomes that audits do not reward
questions.explanation: 作者指出机构会优化被审计指标，可推断未纳入的结果容易得不到资源。
questions.evidence_text: What is omitted can guide investment just as strongly as what is included, because organizations optimize the indicators against which they are audited.

questions.question: Why are understandable draft summaries important?
options: They enable non-specialists affected by a rule to participate meaningfully
They allow laboratories to avoid competent testing
They guarantee that no operator will face compliance costs
They replace the need for technical language in final standards
questions.explanation: 参与者包括消费者、工人和社区，通俗摘要使其能理解并反馈标准后果。
questions.evidence_text: Drafts should be available in understandable summaries, not only specialist language.

title: When Public Services Follow the Person
source_title: China moves to provide basic public services based on residence
source_verification: 页面可访问；核验了基本公共服务从户籍地转向常住地供给，随迁子女教育、公租房、就业地社保、居住证参加居民医保，以及常住人口与财政、设施布局协同等事实。
adaptation_note: 题材参考所列新华社英文网公开事实；本站原创改写，非媒体原文，非历年真题。
content:
A worker may spend years in a city where her child attends school, her income is earned and her medical needs arise, yet key public services have traditionally been tied to household registration elsewhere. Providing basic services by habitual residence seeks to align administrative responsibility with lived geography. The principle is simple; the institutional consequences are not.

Population inflow changes both demand and finance. A receiving district needs classrooms, clinics, rental housing and social workers before all residents hold local registration. If transfers and land allocations rely on outdated registered-population counts, local authorities face an incentive to restrict access or allow quality to decline. Funding formulas must follow credible resident data while protecting privacy and accounting for seasonal or circular mobility. Origin areas also need adjustment as populations age or shrink rather than assuming their existing facilities remain appropriately sized.

Portability creates another layer. Social insurance joined at the place of work, medical coverage based on a residence permit and cross-region settlement reduce discontinuity only if records can be recognized across systems. Technical interoperability is necessary, but errors require human appeal. A mismatched identity field should not leave a patient financing treatment while databases argue. Residents need a visible authority responsible for correction, deadlines and provisional access during disputes.

Equal basic service does not require every city to offer identical extras, but the boundary between a basic entitlement and a local enhancement must be clear. Gradient provision can manage scarce resources, yet waiting rules should be published and should not quietly recreate registration barriers through impossible residence documents. Children, older people and persons with disabilities face particular harm when proof requirements interrupt continuous care or education.

Mobility also complicates democratic accountability. Residents who lack local registration may use services but feel weakly represented in planning them. Consultation, complaint and community participation should follow residence too. Data can show where people live; it cannot by itself reveal inconvenient opening hours, discriminatory treatment or fear of applying.

Reform succeeds when a move no longer repeatedly resets a person's relationship with public institutions. That requires money, records, facilities and voice to follow population change in coordinated ways. Residence-based provision is therefore not merely a new eligibility rule. It is a commitment to redesign administrative geography around the continuity of human lives.

questions.question: What does residence-based service provision require beyond changing eligibility?
options: Immediate identical services in every city
Coordinated reform of funding, data, facilities, appeals and participation
Ending all use of population records
Transferring every origin-area facility to receiving districts
questions.explanation: 文章从财政、设施、跨系统记录、纠错、基本权利边界和居民参与说明这是系统性行政重构。
questions.evidence_text: Residence-based provision is therefore not merely a new eligibility rule.

questions.question: What protection should exist while a records dispute is unresolved?
options: Automatic cancellation of medical coverage
A requirement to return to the registration city
Provisional access plus a responsible correction authority and deadline
Permanent reliance on database decisions
questions.explanation: 第三段明确要求可见纠错责任主体、期限以及争议期间的临时服务准入。
questions.evidence_text: Residents need a visible authority responsible for correction, deadlines and provisional access during disputes.

questions.question: What does “Portability” mean in paragraph three?
options: The physical movement of a clinic building
The seasonal size of a registered population
The freedom of cities to define every service differently
The ability of rights and records to remain usable across places or systems
questions.explanation: 该段讨论工作地参保、居住证医保和跨地区结算的连续性，故指权益记录可跨地使用。
questions.evidence_text: Portability creates another layer.

questions.question: Why can outdated population counts weaken service equality?
options: Resources may not reach districts serving the actual resident population
Origin areas always receive too little funding
Registered residents use no local facilities
Privacy rules prevent any funding transfer
questions.explanation: 作者指出流入地需求先增加，若财政仍按旧户籍人数配置，就会产生限准入或降质量激励。
questions.evidence_text: If transfers and land allocations rely on outdated registered-population counts, local authorities face an incentive to restrict access or allow quality to decline.

questions.question: Why should participation also follow residence?
options: Administrative data already captures every service problem
People affected by local services need influence over their design even without local registration
Only registered residents experience discriminatory treatment
Community planning is unrelated to public-service continuity
questions.explanation: 末段指出实际使用服务的非本地户籍居民可能在规划中代表不足，因此参与权也应基于居住事实。
questions.evidence_text: Residents who lack local registration may use services but feel weakly represented in planning them.
